4. The suit land including the mango garden originally belonged to the CS recorded tenant, Ramani Kanta Sarkar, who planted the mango trees on the suit land. After his death, his three sons transferred 2.85 acres of land to the plaintiffs by the kabala dated 24-5-1958. On 28-5-1958 CS recorded tenant's successive heirs sold 95 decimals of land to the plaintiffs and on 28-9-1959 three successive heirs of the CS recorded tenant sold 95 decimals of land to the plaintiffs and thus in the aforesaid manner the plaintiffs acquired the suit land. During revisional survey a part of the suit land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and a portion of the suit land was recorded in the name of the successive heirs of the said CS recorded tenant whose shares were subsequently purchased in the name of the plaintiffs by their father when they were minor and possession of the land so purchased was made over to the plaintiffs father. During the war of liberation plaintiffs father and some other relatives were killed and because of such disaster plaintiffs were in a perplexed state of mind and, as such, they had difficulty in exercising effective control over the suit land. In the middle of July, 1990 while the officials of the Forest Department came to pluck mango, the plaintiffs protested to that and they then came to know for the first time that the Forest Department acquired the control and management of  the suit land by a notification under the Private Forests Act, 1945. It is also alleged that neither the plaintiffs nor their predecessors-in-interest had any knowledge about the gazette notification vesting control and management of the suit land in the Forest Department nor any notice was ever served on them to show cause against such vesting. It is also asserted by the plaintiffs that the suit land is a mango garden from a long time past and it was neither a private forest nor a waste land. Hence, the taking over, control and management of the suit land under the Private Forests Act, 1945 and also under the Forests Act, 1927 was illegal. The plaintiffs accordingly, made a representation to the Ministry of Forest on August 9, 1990 to return the suit land to them but received no response. The plaintiffs thereafter represented to the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur on 4-1-1992 for handing over the management of the mango garden to them but did not have the desired result. The plaintiffs then represented to the Forest Department for releasing the suit land and thereupon a report was called for and the date of hearing was fixed on 30-3-1992 in this regard. But the Forest Department at the same time also fixed 28-3-1992 for auction of the mango garden. The plaintiffs having found no prospect of release of the suit land filed the suit. 

 5. The defendant Nos. 1-3 and 5 contested the suit by filing joint written statement denying the material allegations contending, inter alia, that since the owners of the suit land failed to raise any objection pursuant to the notices issued on them under the Private Forests Act, the Government by issuing notification dated 3-6-1958 under sections 7 and 11 of the said Act vested control of the suit land in the Regional Forest Officer and since then the defendants have been treating the suit land as a vested forest and continuing to manage the same. The Forest Department thereafter regularly put the said mango garden on auction between 1976-1993. The plaintiffs, however, made representations to the Deputy Commissioner, Dinajpur as well as to the Ministry of Forest for release and return of the suit land to them but their prayer was turned down. The plaintiffs have no title, interest and possession in the suit land and accordingly they manufactured false documents and filed the suit with a view to grabbing the suit land. 

 6. The trial Court decreed the suit. The contesting defendants thereafter took appeal and the appellate Court upon reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court dismissed the suit. The plaintiffs then moved the High Court Division in revision and thereupon the High Court Division on consideration of the arguments advanced by both the sides decreed the suit by reversing the judgment and decree of the appellate Court on the ground that the suit land not being forest or waste land was not liable to be vested in the Government for control and management and also that the requisite notices were also not served on the plaintiffs or their predecessors-in-interest inviting objection as envisaged under the Private Forests Act, 1945 and the Forests Act, 1927. 

 7. Leave was granted to consider the submissions that the suit land having been vested in the Government as forest land by gazette notification No. 768/For/dated 3-6-1958 under the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945 for 100 years and the Forest Department having taken over the possession of the same exercised control and management over it as forest land, the High Court Division erred in law in decreeing the suit by making the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below by dismissing the suit which was decreed by the trial Court on the ground that the suit land being a mango garden not being a forest or waste land was not liable to be vested in the Forest Department for proper conservation and management. 

 8. The short fact leading to the filing of the aforesaid Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 645 of 2001 is that the respondents, Md Nazibar Rahman Talukder and others, as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 178 of 1977 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Rangpur for declaration of plaintiffs' title to the suit land measuring 25.32 and 2.73 acres as described in the schedule Ka and Kha to the plaint. The suit land originally belonged to Taher Mahmud and Hanif Mahmud. The plaintiffs are the heirs and lineal descendants of the said original owners, Taher Mahmud and Hanif Mahmud. The plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the suit land as per their respective share by amicable arrangement among themselves. The suit land was jungle land and the same was so described in CS Khatian and recorded in the name of the predecessors of the plaintiffs. Ultimately, the plaintiffs and their co-sharers cleared the jungle of the suit land in the year 1348 BS and made the same a cultivable land and since then the plaintiffs have been in possession of the same by amicable arrangement amongst themselves and with other co-sharers. The plaintiffs came to know on 3-9-1977 when the government attempted to lease out the suit land on the pretext that the government by notification under the Private Forests Act, 1945 took over the suit land for proper management and control as private forest. The plaintiffs did not know about the said notification and they were and still are in possession of the suit land. But the Karmacharies of the defendants collusively got the suit land recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the SA record. After knowing about the wrong SA record in the name of the said defendants in the government, the plaintiffs in the first part of 1973 filed a Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 1973 under section 143(A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which was dismissed for default on 15-6-1976 due to illness of the plaintiff No. 1 as tadbirkarak. Plaintiff No. 1 after recovery from his illness tried to file a Miscellaneous Case for setting aside the said ex parte order of dismissal but due to legal complications the plaintiffs did not file the Miscellaneous Case but instead filed the present suit for declaration of their title in respect of the suit land. 

 9. The defendant Nos. 1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that the suit-land was a forest land up to 1972 and during the war of liberation the plaintiffs and their relations entered into the forest land, cut down the trees and cleared the jungles and made an attempt to cultivate the same for which several cases were filed in the Court of the SDM Rangpur. The defendants took steps to evict the illegal occupants including the plaintiffs from the suit land but they did not succeed in their attempt in evicting the plaintiffs from the suit land. The plaintiffs are illegal occupants in the suit land since 1971. The defendant No.1 issued a notice to the owners to show cause as to why the suit land should not be vested in the government for the purpose of afforestation and after observing all formalities the government issued a notification No. 14253 dated 4-12-1953 vesting management and control of the suit land in the government. The Forest Department took over the possession of the suit land from 1953 and since then the government had been possessing the same. The plaintiffs or the original owners cannot legally claim any title or possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs are unauthorised occupants since 1971 and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 10. The suit was decreed by the trial Court on contest against the contesting defendant Nos. 1-3 and ex parte against the rest declaring title to the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs vide its judgment and decree dated 15-6-1981. Thereafter, the defendants preferred first appeal in the High Court Division and the High Court Division dismissed the appeal by the impugned judgment on the ground that the suit is not barred by limitation, the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land and the defendant government has failed to prove producing any document or gazette notification under the Private Forests Act showing taking over or vesting of control and management of the suit land as forest or waste land for afforestation. In this background of the case, the defendants filed the present leave petition. 

 11. Mr Joynul Abedin, the learned Deputy Attorney-General, has argued in both the appeal and leave petition that the Government in exercise of its power under sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945 took over and vested the suit land in the Forest Department for the purpose of proper conservation and scientific management by issuing necessary gazette notification and once such notification was published the suit land should be taken to have been validly taken over by and vested in the Government in the Ministry or Forest. But the learned Judges of the High Court Division have erred in decreeing the suit in both the cases by failing to appreciate this legal position. 

 12. The question that has arisen in these two cases (Civil Appeal No. 330 of 2003 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 645 of 2001) is, whether the suit land was taken over by the government and vested in the Forest Department in exercise of its power under sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945 by publishing necessary notifications in the official Gazette in due observance of the legal formalities envisaged in those sections by providing opportunity to the owners of the suit land to show cause against such taking over and vesting of the suit land in the Forest Department. 

 13. It is noted from the record that the suit lands in both the aforesaid Civil Appeal No. 330 of 2003 and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 645 of 2001 were taken over by the Government for vesting, control and management of the same as private forest or as waste land for afforestation in exercise of power under sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945. But in order for such taking over and vesting of the suit lands in both the cases to be valid and legal the owners of the suit land at the relevant time were required to be called upon to show cause against such taking over and vesting. Sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945 are reproduced below for proper appreciation. 

 "Section 7: Vesting of forest in a Regional Forest Officer—Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 3 and 4 or in sub-section (2) of section 6, if the Provincial Government is satisfied that the conservation of any private forest in a notified area should not be left to the owner thereof, the Provincial Government may, by a notification specifying the reasons for so doing, direct that the control of such forest shall be vested in such Regional Forest Officer for such period as may be specified in the notification; 

 "Section 11—Afforestation of other land. (1) If it appears from the report of a Regional Forest Officer that any waste land which is lying uncultivated for not less than three years is suitable for afforestation and that the owner of such land is unwilling or unable to cultivate it by growing therein agricultural crops, or to use it for the purposes of horticulture to the satisfaction of such officer or to afforest it, the Provincial Government may, by a notification, direct that the control of such land shall be vested in the Regional Forest Officer to be specified in the notification for the purpose of afforestation for such period as may be stated in the notification: 

 Provided that the Provincial Government shall not issue any notification under this sub-section without considering whether or not such land can more advantageously be used for the purposes of agriculture or horticulture than for the purposes of afforestation. 

 Provided further that no such notification shall be published until a notice has been issued by such Regional Forest Officer calling upon the owner of such land and any other person interested therein to show cause before the Appellate Committee within such period as may be specified in the notice why the notification should not be published and until the cause, if any, shown and any evidence that may have been produced in support of the same before the Appellate Committee and the opinion of the Appellate Committee thereon have been considered by the Provincial Government. 

 (3) When all expenses incurred by the Provincial Government for the afforestation of any such land have been recouped, the profits resulting from such afforestation shall, during the period the control of such land remains vested in a Regional Forest Officer, be divided in equal shares between the Provincial Government and the owner of the land." 

 14. The bare reading of the law shows that the Government has the power under section 7 to vest control of private forests in a notified area in the Forest Department for the purpose of conservation. Government has also similar power under section 11 to vest control of the waste land in the Forest Department for the purpose of afforestation. In both the cases vesting of control of the aforesaid category of land has to be made by publishing notification in official Gazette after issuing show cause notices on the owners of the land and on due consideration of their objections, if any. 

 15. We have noticed in both the cases that the defendant government has failed to prove that the required show cause notices were ever served on and received by the owners of the suit lands. We have also noted from the record that the defendant Government has also been unsuccessful in proving possession in the suit land in the leave petition. Since sections 7 and 11 are designed to divest the owners of the suit lands of their ownership and possession in the suit lands the same should be strictly interpreted and applied. The defendant Government has failed to discharge its burden of proof that the suit lands were taken over and vested in the Forest Department of the Government by issuing required show cause notices on the owners of the suit lands inviting objection and on due consideration of the objections, if any, raised by the owners: The learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government submits that since the defendant Government has succeeded in producing the Gazette Notifications issued under sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945 the Government should be taken to have issued necessary show cause notices on the owners of the suit lands inviting objection and taken over and vested the suit lands in the Forest Department in due consideration of the objections of the owners of the suit lands, even in the absence of any such notices having been produced and proved before the Court. We do not find force in this contention. In both the cases Courts below have found on evidence that the lands taken over by the aforesaid Gazette notifications were not the category of lands liable to be taken over and vested in the Forest Department under the law. The said notifications are therefore ultra vires the law. We are therefore of the view that the taking over and vesting of the suit lands covered by the aforesaid Civil Appeal and Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal were not made in due compliance of the mandatory requirements under sections 7 and 11 of the Private Forests Act, 1945. In this view of the matter, the taking over and vesting of the suit lands in the Forest Department by the Government by the aforesaid gazette notifications dated 3-6-1958 and 3-9-1953 in the aforesaid appeal and the leave petition respectively have not been proved and they remain merely as a paper transaction.
